title: US Blacklists Sam Altman's Old Y Combinator China Pick Over Startup Built On Stolen Google AI Secrets
desc:
US Blacklists Sam Altman's Old Y Combinator China Pick Over Startup Built On Stolen Google AI Secrets

Of all the people who could end up on a US sanctions list for bankrolling stolen Google AI technology, a former Microsoft executive hand-picked by Sam Altman to run Y Combinator's China arm was probably not on many bingo cards. And yet here we are.

On Monday, the State Department blacklisted Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, the AI startup founded by convicted ex-Google engineer Linwei Ding, along with MiraclePlus, the Chinese venture firm founded by ex-Microsoft AI scientist Lu Qi, and three MiraclePlus-managed funds, for providing seed financing to Zhisuan. According to Bloomberg, the measures may include freezing US assets and banking restrictions.

The best part of the story is Lu's resume, which reads like a tour of every major tech power center of the past 20 years: the stuff corporate espionage movie scripts are made of. Per Bloomberg:

Lu, a former Microsoft executive, was recruited in 2017 by Baidu Inc. to oversee the Chinese search leader's AI efforts, only to quit a year later citing personal reasons. In 2018, Lu – recruited by then-Y Combinator President Sam Altman – joined the US firm to help create YC China.

When Y Combinator abandoned the expansion a year later, Lu and his team simply kept going under the MiraclePlus brand. That's the same MiraclePlus that, according to the State Department, gave a Chinese startup seed money in exchange for equity after its founder showed up touting his inside knowledge of Google's AI infrastructure.

"An Important Missing Piece Of Our Puzzle"

Some quick background on Lu Qi (who also goes by Qi Lu, depending on which side of the Pacific is writing the press release). After rising to executive vice president of engineering at Yahoo, Lu was personally recruited by Steve Ballmer to Microsoft, where he ran Bing, Office and Skype and later helped shape Satya Nadella's AI and bots strategy. In January 2017, Baidu poached him as group president and COO to run its AI push. He lasted 16 months, leaving in May 2018 for "personal and family reasons" and which, as CNBC reported at the time, really meant he just wanted to spend more time in the US.

Three months later he had a new job. In August 2018, Altman's Y Combinator announced Lu would lead YC China (as well as YC's research arm and a new research center in Seattle), with Altman (who just like Ballmer, personally recruited Lu) calling China "an important missing piece of our puzzle."

Well, the puzzle didn't stay assembled for long. In November 2019, in the middle of the trade war, YC pulled the plug on China. Lu spun the team out as MiraclePlus (Qiji Chuangtan in Chinese), which has since become one of China's busiest early-stage investors: it writes $300K checks for 7% stakes and runs two cohorts a year. Its portfolio includes some of China's hottest AI names, among them AI inference platform SiliconFlow and robotics maker AgiBot, both of which are considering Hong Kong listings (and both of which now have a sanctioned backer, which is probably not the line the bankers wanted in the prospectus).

"Replicate Google's Technology... To Fit China's National Conditions"

So how did a Beijing incubator end up on the same list as the guy who walked out of Google with its AI supercomputer blueprints?

According to the State Department fact sheet, Ding applied to MiraclePlus's incubation program on behalf of Zhisuan, "touting his experience with and knowledge of Google's technology and internal systems" and claiming Zhisuan could replicate Google's "super intelligence" infrastructure technology. State says Ding used the program to pitch his ability to replicate Google's technology to fit China's national conditions, and that "MiraclePlus gave seed capital in exchange for an ownership stake in Zhisuan."

That pitch will sound familiar to regular readers. When we first covered Ding's arrest back in March 2024, the indictment quoted a WeChat promo for his Shanghai startup, in which he bragged:

"We have experience with Google's ten-thousand-card computational power platform; we just need to replicate and upgrade it—and then further develop a computational power platform suited to China's national conditions."

In other words, the business plan was the stolen goods. You'd think a seasoned VC might have asked one or two follow-up questions about where the "experience" came from.

MiraclePlus, for its part, denies investing in Zhisuan at all. In a statement on Tuesday, the firm said the sanctions were imposed without any prior communication, and that it is in talks with relevant parties to have them lifted and expects the matter to be resolved through "candid communication." Which, coming from a firm called MiraclePlus, may take a miracle of its own.

The penalties were imposed under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act (PAIPA), signed into law in January 2023 to go after foreign beneficiaries of US trade-secret theft. In addition to Zhisuan and MiraclePlus (formally Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management), the list includes MiraclePlus's Phase I and Phase II venture funds and an entity wholly owned by Phase I. Put differently, Washington went after the money too.

Apple Notes, A Borrowed Badge And A One-Way Ticket

As for the man, the Ding saga has been a long one. Between May 2022 and April 2023, the Google software engineer uploaded more than 2,000 pages of confidential AI trade secrets to his personal Google Cloud account, covering the architecture of Google's custom TPU chips, its GPU systems, the software that orchestrates thousands of chips into a supercomputer, and a custom SmartNIC used for high-speed networking. In other words, the crown jewels of Google's AI stack.

The method was low-tech to the point of comedy: Ding copied the data into the Apple Notes app on his Google-issued MacBook, converted it to PDFs and uploaded those. He also had a colleague scan his access badge so it looked like he was working from Google's US office while he was actually in China. He secretly affiliated himself with two China-based AI companies while still on Google's payroll, applied to a Shanghai government "talent plan" promising to help China build "computing power infrastructure capabilities that are on par with the international level," and downloaded more files less than two weeks before resigning in December 2023. Then he booked a one-way ticket to Beijing.

When the charges first dropped, we couldn't resist pointing out the obvious problem with stealing from Google in the Gemini era:

An ex-Google engineer was charged with stealing artificial intelligence technology while secretly working with two companies based in China. So China's AI is now racist, woke and wrong about everything

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) March 6, 2024

The case later became Exhibit A in what Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang called China's "open secret" tech-theft operation (Jun 14, 2025), in which Wang argued that China is on par with the US on algorithms "because of large-scale espionage."

Fourteen Convictions, One Year

On January 29, a San Francisco jury convicted Ding on seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of trade secret theft, which on paper carried a maximum of 15 years and 10 years per count, respectively. Then the case started to deflate.

In August, Judge Vince Chhabria tossed all seven espionage convictions, ruling there was insufficient evidence Ding intended to benefit the Chinese government (as opposed to just Chinese companies, which apparently is a different thing). And on September 1, he was sentenced to 12 months minus one day, plus two years of supervised release, about $198,000 in restitution to Google and a $2,500 fine. Prosecutors had asked for 70 months; the defense wanted three months of home confinement.

"The idea of a non-custodial sentence is very hard to swallow for me," Chhabria said, which tells you how close Ding came to serving his time from the couch. For context, $198,000 in restitution for the blueprints of Google's TPU stack, which is precisely what anyone trying to build an AI supercomputer without access to Nvidia's best chips would want, is what one might call a bargain.

Which is probably why Washington is now going after the money instead. If the courts won't make the penalty sting for the engineer, the State Department can at least make it sting for whoever funded him.

Beijing, naturally, is not amused. On Tuesday China's commerce ministry expressed "firm opposition" to the sanctions, urged the US to "correct its erroneous practice," and threatened unspecified "necessary measures." The ministry also insisted China's AI achievements are the result of long-term basic research and open cooperation, and have "nothing to do with the so-called 'stealing of trade secrets.'" Sure.

Altman's China Problem, Then And Now

None of this is Altman's fault, of course: he hired a Microsoft and Baidu veteran with a sterling resume in 2018, and YC exited China a year later. MiraclePlus's alleged Zhisuan deal came four years after that. Still, the irony is hard to miss.

The same Altman who once called China the "missing piece" of YC's puzzle spent last month lining up with Dario Amodei and Elon Musk to ask Washington for embedded evaluators, an antitrust waiver and a talk with Beijing, while China goes full send, as we discussed in "'Pace The Frontier': Amodei, Altman & Musk Team Up Against The AI Singularity While China Goes Full Send". Meanwhile, OpenAI is busy defending itself against Apple's lawsuit alleging that OpenAI misused Apple's hardware trade secrets after hiring its former VP of iPhone and Apple Watch product design. Trade secrets, it seems, are having a moment.

The Real Penalty Lands On The Cap Table

The sanctions themselves are probably more symbolic than crippling. MiraclePlus is a Beijing-based firm investing in Chinese startups, and its exposure to the US banking system is likely limited. But the signal matters: for the first time in this case, Washington is targeting the capital behind the theft as well as the thief, and it is doing so with a law built for exactly that purpose.

The more interesting question is what happens next to the MiraclePlus portfolio. SiliconFlow and AgiBot are both eyeing Hong Kong IPOs, and global investors tend to get nervous when a company's early backer is on a US sanctions list, regardless of what the backer says about "candid communication." We suspect the lawyers for those deals are having a busy week.

As for Ding, a jury found he stole Google's AI crown jewels, a judge gave him a year, and his alleged backers got blacklisted. Something tells us the next would-be Ding will look at that math and decide the risk-reward is still pretty attractive.

title: "The State Does Not Create Wealth; It Consumes It": Europe's Socialist Model Hits The Wall
desc:
"The State Does Not Create Wealth; It Consumes It": Europe's Socialist Model Hits The Wall

Authored by Daniel Lacalle via dlacalle.com,

Decades of bloated government, entitlements, subsidies, and mass migration have destroyed Europe's competitiveness and growth, all paid for with ever-rising taxes and more debt. They have also created enormous social discontent. Taxpayers are exhausted, and the recipients of subsidies are looting and vandalizing the streets. The flames in French cities are the bill that is arriving.

On Saturday 17 October, France burned again. What began as marches against the cost of living and the state of public schools turned into the worst violence the country has seen in decades. According to the French government, 550,000 people took to the streets, 1,200 were arrested, and 150 police officers were injured. In Limoges, rioters set the city hall ablaze; in Marseille, they broke into the city hall; and in Lyon, they torched the tourist office. AFP reporters on the ground described scenes more intense than the 2023 riots and the Yellow Vest protests of 2018 and 2019, six months before a presidential election. Major cities, including Paris, Marseille, and Lille, suffered enormous commercial damage with smashed shopfronts, shattered glass, and ransacked retail spaces. In Bordeaux, Mayor Thomas Cazenave reported that up to 100 stores were looted in his city alone.

The riot images will be explained away as the work of a violent fringe, and it will be said that the mob that loots luxury boutiques and supermarkets certainly does not represent the hundreds of thousands who marched peacefully. However, the anger is real, and it has a cause.

Europe has spent half a century building the largest welfare state in the world on the promise that government could guarantee prosperity, security, and equality for everyone. That model has completely failed, and the people who were promised everything are discovering that the state only delivers stagnation and impoverishment.

France is the clearest example of what "democratic socialism" does to a rich nation. France is the most state-heavy economy in the European Union. French public spending reached 57.2% of GDP in 2025, the second highest in the EU and 7.7 points above the average. Its tax burden is among the highest in the world, at 45.3% of GDP in 2024, behind only Denmark in the EU. Public debt rose to 119% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, and the deficit stood at 5.1% of GDP in 2025. If big government, high taxes, and immigration delivered prosperity and social peace, France would be paradise. Instead, the protesters on the streets of Paris are demanding more of the same medicine that made them sick.

The welfare machine eats the economy.

France is not an extreme or single example. The disease is continental. Government expenditure in the European Union reached 49.5% of GDP in 2025 and 49.8% in the euro area. Half of the economy is directly controlled by the state, and much of the rest is regulated, subsidized, or taxed to the point of exhaustion. Social protection benefits alone reached 4,925 billion euros in 2024, 27.3% of the EU's GDP, after growing 6.9% in a single year while nominal GDP grew only 4.4%.

Add the subsidies. European governments spent 340 billion euros on energy subsidies in 2024 and another 168 billion euros in state aid. Governments first make energy expensive with taxes, regulations, and ideological mandates, then subsidize the very costs they created, and finally borrow to pay for the subsidies. Citizens pay three times, as consumers, as taxpayers, and as the future holders of the debt.

The debt is the inevitable consequence. Greece ended 2025 with public debt at 146.1% of GDP, Italy at 137.1%, France at 115.6%, Belgium at 107.9%, and Spain at 100.7%. And those figures hide the largest liability of all. According to Eurostat, the pension entitlements already accrued in social insurance schemes reach 500% of GDP in Spain, 462% in Austria, 438% in Italy, 397% in France, and 347% in Germany, almost all of them unfunded, according to Eurostat. These are promises that no government can keep without crushing the next generation with taxes or destroying the purchasing power of the currency.

Germany, once the engine of Europe, now transfers 127.4 billion euros from the federal budget to its pension system in 2026, rising to 132 billion in 2027. Spain's Social Security debt has almost quadrupled since 2018, from 34,888 million to 136,176 million euros, and social contributions cover pension payments only until early October. The welfare state now lives on borrowing against the future rather than on what the economy produces.

Competitiveness destroyed

There is no free lunch. Every euro of spending must be paid for by the productive economy, and Europe's productive economy is suffocating. The International Monetary Fund expects the euro area to grow just 1.1% in 2026, compared with 2.3% in the United States, with France at a miserable 0.4% and Italy at 0.8%. Labor productivity per hour worked in the EU stood at only 78.5% of the US level in 2024, and in 2025 it grew just 0.4% compared with 1.6% in the United States.

German industrial production has fallen every year since 2022, and the BDI industry association no longer expects a recovery in 2026, only stagnation. Output in energy-intensive sectors is at its lowest level since the end of 2023. That is what happens when energy is made artificially expensive, labor is taxed at confiscatory rates, regulation multiplies, and capital flees.

Inflation makes the situation even worse. Euro area inflation rose to 3.8% in September 2026, with energy prices up 18.9% year-on-year. Governments that printed and borrowed their way through every crisis now discover that the real wages of their citizens cannot keep up. The cost-of-living crisis that sent hundreds of thousands into French streets has its roots in decades of too much government, not too little.

Mass migration worsens the situation.

Instead of reforming, European governments chose to import the illusion of growth. On January 2025, 46.7 million people living in the EU had been born outside it, 10.4% of the population, and the number of non-EU citizens rose by 1.6 million in a single year to 30.6 million. Immigration may be a powerful engine of prosperity when it is carefully selected for skills and enters flexible labor markets with low taxes and limited welfare. Europe did the opposite. It combined mass migration with rigid labor markets, enormous taxes, and the most excessive welfare benefits on the planet.

The result was predictable. Many immigrants have no incentive to adapt or participate and are trapped in low-wage jobs and welfare dependency. Thus, public services were stretched beyond capacity, housing became unaffordable in the major cities, and integration failed in entire neighborhoods. Governments used headline GDP inflated by population growth to hide stagnant income per person, while workers saw their wages fall in real net terms as inflation and their taxes rise. This is the evidence of a model that promised everything to everyone and delivered disappointment to all.

When you create a state big enough to promise everything, it delivers almost nothing but takes away everything it can.

Angry taxpayers, entitled mobs

Democratic socialism created two angry Europeans. The first is the angry taxpayer, the middle-class worker, the small business owner, and the self-employed professional who pays more every year and receives worse services, longer waiting lists, unaffordable housing, security problems, and a pension system that will not be there when they retire. The second is entitled Europe, a constituency that has been taught for decades that the state owes it everything and responds to inevitable disappointment with rage and violence.

Both are victims of the same lie. Politicians promised that they could raise taxes on the rich, borrow without limit, and expand entitlements forever with no consequences. They told voters that someone else would pay. Now that someone else, the productive economy, is exhausted. Capital is leaving, young talent is emigrating, industry is closing, and the bill is landing on the middle class and on young people who will inherit the debt.

What Europe needs is less state. Another subsidy, another tax on «the rich» or another emergency fund financed with joint debt will only deepen the crisis. The way forward is to cut unproductive spending, reduce the tax burden on labor and investment, end the subsidy culture that keeps the economy zombified, liberalize markets, and abandon the ideological mandates that have made European industry uncompetitive.

Europe needs a migration policy designed for prosperity rather than electoral calculation, selective, linked to employment, and not to welfare entitlement. It needs a gradual transition from unfunded pay-as-you-go pensions to capitalized systems in which workers own their savings, as Sweden and the Netherlands have shown is possible.

Citizens need to realize the truth, which is that the state does not create wealth; it consumes it.

The riots in France are a warning to America. When a society is told for decades that it is entitled to everything and then discovers that the state is broke, the result is not solidarity but violence.

Democratic socialism promised Europe equality and security. It delivered stagnation, inflation, debt, and rage. If America adopts this system, it will follow the same path of misery and desperation. The sooner Europe abandons democratic socialism, the sooner it can recover the prosperity that made it the envy of the world.

title: "Not To My Knowledge": Ilhan Omar Can't Quite Rule Out Marrying Her Brother In Wild Interview... And Trump Noticed
desc:
"Not To My Knowledge": Ilhan Omar Can't Quite Rule Out Marrying Her Brother In Wild Interview... And Trump Noticed

As the investigation into whether Ilhan Omar married her brother to scam US immigration, the Minnesota Democrat just stepped in it, big time.

In her first interview since Homeland Security Investigations agents searched her Washington home last week, the Minnesota Democrat sat down with MS NOW's Chris Hayes, about as friendly a venue as exists on cable. She called the decade-old claim that her ex-husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is her brother "insane." Then Hayes gave her the layup, asking whether there was some "weird kernel of truth" to it. Her answer was "Not to my knowledge."

Regular readers will recall that earlier this week we flagged a report that federal investigators are using DNA to probe the "married her brother" claim. So the timing could have been better. The clip went everywhere within the hour:

YIKES: Ilhan Omar was just asked if she married her brother on Live TV

Her answer: "Not to my knowledge..."

WHAT?!

She can't even say "NO"?!

What other person would answer this question like that?

Things are about to get bad for Ilhan. pic.twitter.com/n8wwJb4puy

— Benny Johnson (@bennyjohnson) October 22, 2026

In other words, the one question her own side's friendliest interviewer was guaranteed to ask is the one she didn't answer with a "no." Below we walk through what she actually said, how fast the White House pounced, and why "not to my knowledge" is a strange hill to stand on with a federal grand jury in the background.

"Which Is Insane"

Omar claims the allegation started on a Somali blog and was picked up by "right-wing conspiracy theorists in Minneapolis":

"...they just kind of went and found random people who were like, 'She introduced us. She introduced him to us and said he was her brother.' Which is insane."

HAYES: "He was not - you were not related to him at all? Not that there's not some weird kernel of truth that through some-"

OMAR: "Not to my knowledge."

The generous reading is that Hayes's question was oddly phrased (a "kernel of truth" through "some" mechanism) and Omar was hedging against a hypothetical rather than admitting anything. The less generous reading is that when the stakes are denaturalization, people tend to choose their words very carefully. Make of that what you will.

"That's An Answer A Lot Of Us Assume"

It took the president about an hour and a half. After his South Carolina rally, Trump was asked about the clip, according to Townhall:

🚨 LMFAO! President Trump just FLAMED Ilhan Omar for answering "NOT TO MY KNOWLEDGE" when asked if she married her brother

"Yeah, well 'not to my knowledge'... that's NOT a good answer. That's an answer a LOT of us assume." 🤣

She's TOTALLY cooked! 😂 https://t.co/Mljre01LVM pic.twitter.com/GpHvia7rh2

— Nick Sortor (@nicksortor) October 22, 2026

That's an answer that a lot of us assume." The rest of the online right was less restrained, and we will spare readers most of it.

Omar's brother hasn't made it easy on her. In a 2012 Instagram post after Ilhan's daughter was born, her brother/husband posted "Nieces, fresh out of the vagina!"

About That Raid

The brother line overshadowed the rest of a fairly revealing interview. According to the New York Post, Omar said:

  • Agents "went room by room" and "took 17 items," including cellphones, her daughter's old phone, her husband's notebooks, a Somali phrase book and a camera.

title: Creepy Ad Tells Grandparents To Get Consent Before Hugging Their Own Grandkids
desc:
Creepy Ad Tells Grandparents To Get Consent Before Hugging Their Own Grandkids

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

A publicly funded advert from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's We-Consent campaign shows grandparents arriving at the front door. One grandchild rushes in for a hug. The other winces and recoils as the older couple lean in. The voiceover declares: "Not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely."

This is not a measured reminder about bodily autonomy. It is a deliberate attempt to plant suspicion inside ordinary homes, cast grandparents as potential abusers, and train the next generation to treat spontaneous family affection as something that requires official clearance.

The same ideological current that wants to erase the words "mother" and "father," rewrite sex education as social engineering, and replace "husband and wife" with sterile inclusive language is now targeting the simple act of a grandmother putting her arms around a grandchild.

?? Ireland is basically telling grandparents that a hug from Nana requires a consent form. The republic has launched a consent campaign ad warning grandparents not to assume their grandchildren want a squeeze. Is the “Irish goodbye” being replaced by the “Irish hello”? Writer: Marie https://t.co/92rg9ifarr

— Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal) October 21, 2026

The 25-second clip is part of the broader We-Consent programme funded by the Department of Justice and aims, in its own words, to inform and educate the public about "all forms of consent" across every relationship.

In practice it has produced a video that visually distorts the grandparents' approach so they appear threatening.

The indoctrination is getting really weird.

— Paul Joseph Watson (@PrisonPlanet) October 21, 2026

Also, as Graham Linehan pointed out, the makers of the advert even managed to crowbar in a diverse grandchild who looks nothing like the grandparents, just for the sake of it.

Why is one of the kids black? Is this about hugging your grandkids or random strangers?

— Graham Linehan (@Glinner) October 21, 2026

On GB News, Patrick Christys reacted with open disbelief, remarking that you would try telling that to his Greek grandmother.

‘Oh come, sweet asteroid of death… you try telling that to my Greek grandma!’ @PatrickChristys is in disbelief at a video released by the Irish state that warns grandparents over hugging their grandchildren. https://t.co/c3KsOC1dDi

— GB News (@GBNEWS) October 21, 2026

The backlash was immediate and cross-party. Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan stated that the video "does not represent the views of the Government," was "both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents," and had been removed by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre after officials engaged with them.

He added: "It goes without saying that having loving grandparents in a child's life is an incredibly positive thing to be cherished and not something to be campaigned against."

He further noted that while consent education around sexual relationships is vital, "this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."

Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín called the advert "bonkers" and said it was "planting the seed that a grandparent's hug may be insidious and a suspicious activity," which he described as "really wrong."

He argued that grandparents possess the "emotional intelligence" to know when a child does not want to be hugged, that the state has no business in this space, and that it "owes grandparents an apology."

Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill labelled the piece "a complete waste of resources," "offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," and "a million miles off the mark." He observed that the distorted imagery gave "a distinct impression of threat" and asked: "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls... before we can greet family members?"

Councillor Gavin Pepper slammed the government and NGOs for "losing the run of ourselves." He wrote that while children should never be forced into unwanted contact, "we also need a bit of common sense." The grandparent-grandchild bond is "one of the most important bonds in Irish family life," and "a hug from a loving grandparent should not be presented as something strange or suspicious." "Irish culture, family and traditions matter."

None of this is an isolated misstep. It sits inside a wider pattern of institutional hostility toward the nuclear and extended family. The same political and cultural forces that fund these campaigns have pushed to strip "mother" and "father" from official language, treat biological reality as optional, and reframe parental authority as a risk to be managed by the state.

The We-Consent campaign's own materials speak of moving "from a Moment to a Movement" and of changing culture so that consent becomes "an integral part" of every interaction. In the grandparents advert that ambition collapses into the grotesque: ordinary love is reframed as a potential violation requiring prior negotiation.

Families that once operated on shared affection, known character, and instinctive boundaries are now to be tutored by state-funded NGOs in the correct way to greet their own kin.

Public money was spent to produce and circulate this video, and the organisations involved saw no problem with casting Irish grandparents as the face of unwanted physical contact. Real sexual violence is a serious crime. Pathologising a grandmother's hug is not a contribution to preventing it. It is a contribution to the long project of making the family itself feel unsafe, contingent, and in need of external supervision.

Parents and grandparents will continue to hug their children. The state can keep commissioning ads that treat that fact as a problem. The rest of the country has already decided which side of that argument is deranged.

title: Italy Makes Parents Pay For Milan Rioters: Meloni Decree Fines Families, Adds Riot Crime Carrying Up To 5 Years
desc:
Italy Makes Parents Pay For Milan Rioters: Meloni Decree Fines Families, Adds Riot Crime Carrying Up To 5 Years

Italy's cabinet approved an emergency decree-law on Oct. 20 in response to the weekend riots in Milan, ANSA reported. The eight-article text creates a new offense of violent participation in demonstrations, extends preventive detention to minors aged 16 and over, and sends 500 more soldiers to Milan through Dec. 31 at a cost of €4.7 million.

Parents of minors who commit violence at demonstrations face fines of €500 to €1,000, and the fine doubles for a repeat. It applies even when the minor is too young to be prosecuted. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said that if a minor is responsible for the damage, the parents should pay, and she asked all political forces to side with legality.

The new crime covers anyone who uses sticks or clubs or throws objects at a protest in a way that endangers people. It carries two to five years in prison and a fine of up to €20,000, with a higher penalty for a covered face or damage to public infrastructure or utilities. Anyone who organizes or promotes groups for violent demonstrations, including through online tools, faces four to 12 years.

For minors, those over 14 are presumed capable of understanding their acts and can be charged immediately, a provision carried over from a bill the cabinet approved in July. Meloni said then that anyone who assaults, robs or wrecks must pay "even if he is 15 or 16," and the opposition called it propaganda and an authoritarian drift. The new decree also lets the police chief bar a group of five or more minors from gathering where they behave in an intimidating way. It also makes a minor injury to a police officer prosecutable automatically and adds optional deferred arrest for property damage.

Violence broke out in Milan after a Saturday demonstration over living costs and public services. Reuters reported that hooded protesters, many believed to be minors, set fires and looted shops including Decathlon and Vodafone while luxury stores on Via Montenapoleone stripped their windows. Police took 271 young people to the Milan police headquarters; 32 were arrested, 23 of them minors. Similar clashes hit Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin. Euronews counted 14 injured officers and a damage estimate from the Confcommercio business group of over €1 million in Milan alone and at least €1.3 million nationwide.

Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said early findings ruled out structured links to antagonist groups, and no organizer has been identified. He called the youth mobilization spontaneous but said "something certainly happened" and that answers would come soon. Defense Minister Guido Crosetto blamed "hybrid warfare," while Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini rejected the idea of a coordinating hand, Russian involvement included. Ynet reported that assessments suggest many participants simply wanted to break things, though police also identified radical-left activists from social centers who left once force was used.

The package was a political negotiation. After a 90-minute summit at Palazzo Chigi on Oct. 19, Il Sole 24 Ore reported that more than 200 young people had been detained and that 80 percent were under 18. Salvini announced "500 more soldiers to defend Milan. A victory for the League," while Forza Italia claimed credit for the same troops. Crosetto's request to give soldiers judicial police powers did not make it into the text, per ANSA, which also reported that tension with the presidential palace delayed the cabinet meeting by almost an hour. The government denied any blockage.

title: A Warning From France
desc:
A Warning From France

Authored by Jeffrey A. Tucker via The Epoch Times,

The chaos in the streets of France has a familiar ring to Americans who watched several cities burn in the summer of 2020. What started as "mostly peaceful" protests were quickly hijacked by chaos actors who whipped up excitable populations into a looting and pillaging frenzy, resulting in police crackdowns in the best cases but utter destruction in the worst cases.

The metaphor of the powder keg is one that is often invoked here. In the U.S. case, we had suffered months of COVID lockdowns that created pent-up energy on the part of an entire generation that had been shut out of schools, spilling into the streets in the name of protesting racism.

Oddly, a media that had been screaming for people to stay home and stay safe flipped on a dime to urge everyone to get out in the streets for purely political protests.

Something similar seems to have happened in France. Rising unemployment, high cost of living, underfunded and failing schools, loss of opportunity, rising crime, and frustration over waves of new immigrant populations have reached a fever pitch. Peaceful protests turned violent with masked and destructive provocateurs lighting fires and pillaging whole commercial sectors in many cities.

It was six years ago that France experimented with some of the toughest lockdowns in Europe. They kept schools open but restricted gatherings of all sorts. Bars, restaurants, and cafés faced particularly long disruptions: closed from mid-March 2020, reopened gradually in June 2020, then closed again from late October 2020 until May and June of 2021. After that, there were long capacity limits. Cultural venues, gyms, and ski resorts were also heavily restricted.

Cities were shut to the unvaccinated. France used the passe sanitaire (health pass: proof of vaccination, recent recovery, or negative test) starting in summer 2021 for restaurants, bars, cinemas, museums, long-distance transport, large events, and shopping centers. From January 2022, this became a passe vaccinal for those over 16 in many of the same places, lasting until suspension on March 2022.

All of this was totalitarian by any standard and it created a fiscal crisis as the state funded the entire mess with huge subsidies and payments to both individuals and businesses. The economy never recovered and business has struggled ever since. In the backdrop of this is one of Europe's most generous and expensive welfare states tangled up with a regulatory apparatus that makes the United States look like a laissez-faire utopia by comparison.

The unemployment problem is particularly poignant for students with advanced degrees as funded by the state. Like the latter years of the Soviet Union, everyone seems to have a high-level credential in something but these pieces of paper are guaranteeing nothing on the real-world job markets.

Then there is the resulting inflation, the worst in 40 years. It was intensified by France's idiotic embrace of net zero policies on energy that have resulted in high prices and rationing. This is the land of austerity, highly controlled, with a ruling class presiding over dramatically declining living standards, a forever rising welfare state, a highly regulated business sector, combined with a disastrous immigration policy that has destabilized demographics.

No French government has balanced its books in 52 years. The parasitic elites have squandered the wealth of the population while closing off opportunities for enterprise and economic growth.

France, more than any other industrialized democracy, has followed the path of Progressive policies in everything. And look where it has gotten them? No one likes the results and absolutely no one trusts the system. French voters keep rejecting establishment politicians but the establishment somehow never leaves. Reform never arrives while frustrations fester.

The 19th-century French economist Frédéric Bastiat long ago nailed the question of the participation in the public life of a nation, explaining why it cannot belong to all but only to those who have the capacity to exercise that right responsibly.

"It is not the voter alone who suffers the consequences of his vote," he wrote, "because each vote touches and affects everyone in the entire community; because the people in the community have a right to demand some safeguards concerning the acts upon which their welfare and existence depend."

Exactly right and this is precisely the problem in which France found itself. It never restricted participation rights even as it flung open the borders and endlessly expanded the welfare state. This is the path to national suicide in any nation.

Is it too late for a political solution? Perhaps but that raises the question of how this chaos will resolve. We could look back to the interwar period in Europe and see one possible path. The inflation and social chaos as fallout from the Great War ended up raising a generation of authoritarian politicians rallying around fascist ideology. We tend to single out Germany but often forget that the same tendencies hit Italy, Spain, and France.

This is the only real modern precedent we have for how this ends. History may not repeat and I've wondered for years if something more dramatic is headed to Europe, something more like 1989 and 1990 in the former Soviet empire. States unraveled in different ways but the result was the same everywhere. An entire establishment and system were washed away in a few short years, discrediting decades of rule.

The states from that period that undertook the biggest reforms - Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovenia, and Soviet satellites Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia - also happened to be the same states that resisted the push for open borders for several decades. They have avoided the economic sclerosis of Europe along with the social, demographic, and industrial decay. It's possible that the next stage of Europe will involve not just the full-scale unraveling of the European Union but also the abrupt overthrow of whole political establishments.

Let France be a warning to America. The policies that inflicted so many wounds on this country are all the same policies advocated in elite and fashionable circles in the United States, pushed by the heights of academia, and celebrated by establishment media. It's all about more controls, more corporate cartels, more regulations, higher taxes, and more immigration floods without any real standards over what constitutes citizenship.

If the United States goes this way - it very well could happen with enough voter apathy and poor policies such as those being imposed on New York City today - we'll end up right where France is today. We face a choice. We can choose chaos or choose to return to the ideals of a constitutional republic that our Founders envisioned. This is not only a fork in the road for France. It points to a coming fork for the United States too.

title: "High Likelihood Of Error": Judge Halts DHS Voter-Fraud Door-Knocks In Nine States
desc:
"High Likelihood Of Error": Judge Halts DHS Voter-Fraud Door-Knocks In Nine States

The Trump administration wanted an AI dragnet for weeding out illegals trying to vote - however a federal judge says it's catching legal citizens in the process and has put a stop to it.

Late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California, a Biden appointee, issued a preliminary injunction barring the Department of Homeland Security from election-related field operations in nine states when the targets are people agents "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens." The ruling lands in a week full of voter-roll news. This morning we reported that the LA County registrar admitted it has no way to check the citizenship of 20,000 voters flagged by DOJ, which came on the heels of the Trump admin's lawsuit against the state.

Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín's core finding on Wednesday, however, was that there was a "high likelihood of error" (California Nurses Association v. Mullin, No. 4:26-cv-10680):

"Even under the best conditions, there is a high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents."

In other words, DHS cannot reliably tell who is a citizen.

Below we walk through how the target lists were built, what the judge actually blocked (it is narrower than the headlines suggest), the administration's case, and why the real deadline is 5pm Friday.

DHS focused their searches on California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The raw material was 48.2 million records received "through independent sources" the judge deemed to have "questionable provenance," plus 50.6 million records from DOJ. Those came from state voter rolls or, where states refused to share, "unreliable commercial versions." DHS then "enriches" the data through a system called iLab, "using unknown artificial intelligence tools." USCIS staff then had to whittle the list down:

"...a minimum of 40 suspected subject reviews, which requires officers to take no more than twelve minutes to eliminate a person from the target list using the commercial databases."

That said, the ruling doesn't mean DHS can't investigate voter fraud.

"Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections."

The order runs until 8:00pm on Nov 3 or when polls close.

title: Netanyahu To IDF: 'Overthrow The Iranian Regime'
desc:
Netanyahu To IDF: 'Overthrow The Iranian Regime'

Authored by Dave DeCamp via AntiWar.com

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that his directive to the Israeli military is to "overthrow the regime in Iran" as he continues to ramp up his rhetoric in the days before the October 27 Israeli elections.

"My directive to the IDF, the Mossad, and the defense establishment… is to overthrow the regime in Iran," Netanyahu told a group of graduating IDF officers, according to The Jerusalem Post.

The Israeli leader went on to claim that Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, is pursuing nuclear weapons, a claim he’s been making about the Islamic Republic for decades.

"The Iranian regime still has not learned its lesson. Mojtaba Khamenei decided to follow in his father’s footsteps and has released the safety catch, and Iran is once again trying to develop weapons of death," he said. "Iran is once again attempting to develop a nuclear bomb."

While both Netanyahu and President Trump continue to frame the conflict as being about preventing a nuclear-armed Iran, there was no evidence either before the June 2025 war or the current war that Tehran had decided to pursue nuclear weapons, and that was the consensus of the US intelligence agencies.

Netanyahu also referenced Trump’s suggestion that the US and Israel will "finish the job" against Iran, something the US president said when endorsing Netanyahu for Israel’s elections.

"And so, as long as they are here, as long as they are willing to join a threatening and terrible weapon, the State of Israel is in existential danger. And our role, the role of all of us, is to save the nation. My good friend, President Trump, also believes that this is the only way," Netanyahu said.

Top MAHA Adviser Calley Means Resigns Amid Reported Frustration Over White House Food-Policy Delays

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

A top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is stepping down.

Calley Means, who has worked on a range of Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiatives, did not disclose a reason for his resignation on Oct. 22, and said he has tremendous respect for both Kennedy and President Donald Trump.

"They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick. More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history - and I know this movement is just getting started," Means wrote on X.

"It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from [food stamps], removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement."

The White House and the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.

Means, 41, founded a company called Truemed in 2022, which focused on letting people spend money from health savings accounts and similar tranches on health products, and later co-authored a book with his sister, Dr. Casey Means.

Early in Trump's second term, Means was a special government employee, advising Kennedy and other officials. He joined the Department of Health and Human Services in late 2025 as a senior adviser.

Means has frequently spoken at press briefings and on social media about steps the Trump administration has taken to clean up food, including banning several synthetic dyes and pressuring companies to voluntarily remove others, and updating the food pyramid.

“I leave with tremendous respect for President Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr.,” he said.

“This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”

Means said he would continue working to further Kennedy’s MAHA agenda.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Means was greatly frustrated by White House delays of some of Kennedy’s most popular policy ideas and blamed others in the administration for allowing food companies and special interests to have too much sway, people familiar with the matter said. One of them described Means as “disillusioned.”

Means declined to comment on the reasons for his departure.

Means’ exit comes after administration officials deferred announcements of two of Kennedy’s food priorities: a definition of ultraprocessed foods aimed at eventually labeling them as such, as well as a regulation mandating less added sugar and more protein in school meals.

In the latest indication that a sea change is underway where US support of Israel is concerned, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) on Wednesday announced it will stop endorsing political candidates and directly contributing to their campaigns and PACs. The move reflects a new political environment in which the receipt of AIPAC money and endorsements is now being exploited as a major political liability.

AIPAC isn't abandoning the political battlefield, but is choosing to emphasize stealthy means of influencing election outcomes. AIPAC will continue operating its cryptically-named United Democracy Project independent super PAC. That entity is prohibited from coordinating with candidates or giving them money, but can spend a limitless amount to promote favored candidates or undermine their opponents.

First reported by Jewish Insider, the major policy shift was disclosed in a letter to AIPAC members. "[The current election cycle is] one of the most challenging environments in recent memory," wrote the group's president, Bernie Kaminetsky, and three other officials. "We assess that the challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead."

Earlier this year, AIPAC suffered an expensive, high-profile loss in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary. The group's super PAC spent more than $30 million on Rep. In recent days, El-Sayed said that, contrary to the long-running characterization, "It's time for us to realize that Israel is not actually our friend...an ally that takes your money to push you into wars you shouldn’t be fighting is not an ally." Recent polls show El-Sayed with a 2-point lead over GOP nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers.

On the other hand, AIPAC also participated in an important victory, as the group helped oust Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie in the GOP primary. Thanks to money spent by AIPAC's United Democracy Project, the Republican Jewish Coalition, and the MAGA Kentucky PAC -- which was created solely to oust Massie and funded by non-Kentuckian Jewish billionaires Miriam Adelson, Paul Singer and John Paulsen -- the contest was the most expensive primary in US House history. Massie earned the Israel lobby's wrath by opposing foreign aid to any country, voting against pro-Israel legislation and condemning Trump's wars on Iran.

title: Iran's Hardliners Push For Nuclear Weapons As U.S. War Drags On
desc:
Iran's Hardliners Push For Nuclear Weapons As U.S. War Drags On

Authored by RFE/RL Staff via OilPrice,

It was once taboo in Iran to publicly speak about developing nuclear weapons. The authorities would often point to former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's religious edict barring the development of weapons of mass destruction. Iranian officials have long insisted the country's nuclear program is solely for civilian purposes.

Open calls for a bomb from sitting lawmakers and senior security officials would have been unthinkable a few years ago. But with the war with the United States in limbo, that's no longer the case.

After almost eight months of conflict and with Washington reportedly weighing strikes on Pickaxe Mountain, a deep underground site where US and Israeli officials say Iran has moved thousands of centrifuges, the talk is even growing.

Kamal Kharazi, an adviser to Khamenei who was killed in Israeli strikes earlier this year, said in 2024 that Tehran "might review our nuclear doctrine" if it felt an existential threat. The US-Israeli war against Iran this year seems to be seen by some as that very existential threat.

Khamenei and a cadre of Iran's top security and military brass were killed in the opening salvo of the war on February 28. While the strikes mostly targeted sites affiliated with the state, the military, or nuclear facilities, civilian infrastructure was also hit and ordinary Iranians killed.

Major US military operations have wound down in favor of economic pressure, including a naval blockade of Iranian ports, and indirect talks through mediators have stalled.

US President Donald Trump rejected Iran's recent proposal for a seven-day cease-fire and a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and he has threatened to resume major strikes. Washington says any deal must include what Vice President JD Vance called a "meaningful" reduction in Iran's uranium enrichment capacity.

Open Calls To Go Nuclear

Iran signed the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) in 1968 and ratified it in 1970. The NPT bars nuclear states from sharing arsenals and obliges non-nuclear states not to build them, while guaranteeing access to peaceful nuclear technology under safeguards.

It also signed the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) with a group of global powers, including the United States, in 2015 that limited Tehran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief.

But since Trump unilaterally pulled the United States out of the accord in 2018, Iran has ramped up its enrichment of uranium, though it continued to claim its nuclear program was purely for civilian purposes.

In June last year, Israel and the United States carried out air strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, warning that Iran was close to developing nuclear weapons. On February 28, the two ramped up the pressure further by launching the air strikes that led to the current war.

Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a lawmaker and member of the parliament's influential National Security and Foreign Policy committee, recently argued that Iran has already paid a price for its nuclear program - and that it's time to produce weapons.

Hossein Ali Haji-Deligani, another lawmaker, described Iran's lack of nuclear deterrence as one of its major weaknesses and suggested a bomb could be tested in the not-too-distant future.

Even Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, suggested pursuing nukes is not off the table. He has blamed Trump's policies for "pushing the world toward acquiring nuclear weapons."

Davud Modarresian, a conservative commentator and proponent of going nuclear, wrote on X that developing a bomb is "more important than food."

He argued that developing a nuclear bomb would serve as "a guarantee of the country's survival," pointing to Trump's comment earlier this month about the importance of maintaining good relations with nuclear powers.

"When people have 11 nuclear missiles, it's nice to get along," Trump said about North Korea and his relations with its leader, Kim Jong Un.

In 2003, Khamenei officially issued a fatwa banning the development, possession, and use of nuclear weapons by Iran under Islamic law.

Modarresian said the fatwa has never really been an obstacle to developing nukes and blamed "indecision and lack of unified political will" for Iran not weaponizing its nuclear program.

But some, at least in public, have pushed back on weaponizing the nuclear program, or what's left of it.

Mohammad Mokhber, a former vice president who currently serves as a senior adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, said Iran already has the deterrence it needs. Speaking on October 19, he credited Tehran's policy of regionalizing the conflict as a strong enough deterrence.

Mokhber also played up Iran's ability to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, saying, "Any country that has the Strait of Hormuz has no need for an atomic bomb." He argued that controlling the chokepoint impacts billions of people whereas a bomb "might kill 50,000 to 100,000 people."

Meanwhile commentators opposed to developing nukes warn about the repercussions of attempting to acquire a bomb.

Sina Jahani, a journalist based in Tehran, argued that abandoning the NPT and producing a nuclear weapon would be "playing into Israel's hands."

Meanwhile, political commentator Amir Ali Abolfath cautioned that Iran's adversaries would learn of any moves to build nukes before Iran could produce them.

"What happens when the country's entire infrastructure is destroyed after a destructive American attack before nuclear deterrence is achieved?" he wrote on X, directing his question to proponents of going nuclear. "Would acquiring an atomic bomb after the destruction of the country still bring deterrence?"

State Of The Nuclear Program

As Iranians argue over whether to weaponize the nuclear program, a more practical question looms: Can Iran actually build a bomb, given the state of its nuclear infrastructure?

Iran's ability to enrich uranium has been crippled, but the core of its nuclear program likely survives.

Of the three enrichment plants, the only aboveground one, at Natanz, was destroyed. The other two, at Natanz and Fordow, were badly damaged and are widely believed to be out of action. Strikes also destroyed Iran's only uranium milling and conversion facilities.

The biggest unknown is the fate of Iran's 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent purity. Rafael Grossi, director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), said back in March that more than 200 kg of that stockpile remains in tunnels at Isfahan, with some at Natanz. The agency said in September that it had lost track of the stockpiles more than a year ago.

US and Israeli officials say Iran moved thousands of centrifuges into Pickaxe Mountain, buried an estimated 80-100 meters deep in granite. Trump last week said Washington "may have to go there."

In theory, as long as Iran is in possession of its highly enriched uranium stockpile, it can enrich it to weapons grade with little effort and just a few centrifuges, which is why the Pickaxe Mountain site has been in the news for a while. Whether it has the ability to produce a bomb, however, is a different matter.

Iran has long rejected the idea of giving up its stockpile but has offered to dilute it as part of a wider agreement with the United States to end the war, now in its eighth month.

Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. is a 69-year-old retired elementary-school teacher who has lived in Petersburg for 46 years and worked for the US Forest Service. He's not related to the senator. Here's where it gets interesting: he's a registered Republican, not a Democrat. He was a member of the Alaska Independence Party and registered as a Republican after that party dissolved late last year, per Newsweek. In June correspondence with state investigators he said he had had no contact with the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola. He has denied being a plant, saying he entered the race out of frustration with the senator.

Alaska News adds that no Division of Elections record supports the claim that Democrats put him up. So the "Dumocrat" plant is a Republican. Brave.

The Courts Already Spoke

This isn't a new fight. Per Newsweek, Alaska's Division of Elections, overseen by Republican Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, moved in June to remove him, concluding his candidacy was intended "to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality." A judge overturned that decision, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in late June that he could stay on the ballot. To tell the two apart, the ballot lists the incumbent as "Sullivan, Dan S." with an incumbent tag and the challenger as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," and leaves the challenger's party line blank.

Under Alaska's top-four primary, he finished third on Aug. 18 with 2.47% (4,107 votes), per state results, which put him on the November ranked-choice ballot. Trump had already warned voters before the primary, calling him an "imposter" and urging Alaskans to "VOTE FOR THE REAL DAN SULLIVAN."

title: Kushner Denies Bombshell Book Claims Of Secret Gulf-Funded Accounts
desc:
Kushner Denies Bombshell Book Claims Of Secret Gulf-Funded Accounts

Jared Kushner is denying explosive allegations that, while serving as a senior White House adviser in Trump's first term, he had access to secret foreign bank accounts stocked with roughly $2 billion from Gulf royals - and that Dutch intelligence watched him use one of them through his hacked iPhone.

The claims come from an excerpt of investigative journalist Matthew Cole's forthcoming book Princes and Thieves, published Thursday by Vanity Fair. Cole alleges that Saudi and Emirati money funded a roughly $750 million account in the UAE that Kushner helped manage as an off-the-books foreign policy fund, and that UAE leader Mohamed bin Zayed moved another roughly $1 billion to Israel for Kushner - money a source told Cole was meant for his "personal benefit."

Cole, a former national security reporter at The Intercept who previously produced investigations for ABC and NBC News, says the reporting took him four years. His book is published by Atria/One Signal, a Simon & Schuster imprint.

October is the month of political surprises. If substantiated, this would be a big one. It's also sure to provide endless headlines after midterms, if (when) Democrats take the House.

Kushner fired back on X. "The allegations made by this author are completely insane, categorically false, and never happened," he wrote. "No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations."

He called the excerpt "a mixture of fantasy, fiction, and advocacy, written by someone who is either deeply disturbed or acting with sinister intent." His lawyer told Cole that "there are no accounts and never were."

.@VanityFair posted an excerpt from a book containing outrageous and categorically false allegations. The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened. We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them. No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations. During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened. These are outrageous fabrications being presented as investigative journalism. This is not journalism. It is a mixture of fantasy, fiction, and advocacy, written by someone who is either deeply disturbed or acting with sinister intent.

— Jared Kushner (@jaredkushner) October 22, 2026

Watched through his iPhone

Here's the story. The usual grains of salt apply.

Cole's account begins in late 2017, when Dutch military intelligence learned that a Russian GRU operative - a dark web hacker specializing in stolen bank data - was headed to the UK. With British cooperation, the Dutch gave him a choice: work for them or face espionage charges. He flipped.

The Russian gave the Dutch access to a GRU server in Rostov, where they found screenshots of Kushner's iPhone. By early 2018, Dutch hackers had found their own way into the phone. They couldn't turn it into a microphone, but they could see his screen. They watched him log into a UAE bank account that had received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, Cole writes.

Cole's first tip, in the spring of 2020, went further. A source told him Kushner appeared to have moved significant sums from the account to people including "a warlord, a mercenary and a one-time hit man." Cole writes that he told the source it sounded preposterous. Six months later, a second source confirmed knowing about Kushner and transfers from a UAE account.

The accounts

According to Cole, the arrangement grew out of a bigger offer. Early in Trump's first term, bin Zayed and Saudi Arabia's Mohammed bin Salman discussed putting more than $10 billion into a slush fund to advance the new administration's foreign policy goals - including, Cole writes, helping pay for Trump's border wall to secure a second term. The idea fizzled.

Instead, the two royals put at least $2 billion into at least two accounts for Kushner, whose family company at the time faced a billion-dollar loan coming due on its flagship Manhattan tower, 666 Fifth Avenue.

The first account, which Cole calls "Alpha," was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, chaired by bin Zayed's brother Tahnoon bin Zayed. Starting in 2017, the Saudis and Emiratis allegedly moved roughly $750 million into it through Azerbaijan, where, Cole writes, some banks will swap riyals or dirhams for dollars for a 6 to 7 percent fee, leaving auditors nothing to trace.

The account belonged to the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a government-funded charity Cole says doubled as a cover for the UAE's secret military and intelligence operations abroad, including weapons purchases. Kushner was allegedly a signatory, with access to a fund he and bin Zayed partly managed as they chased a grand bargain on Israel.

A source who knew of the deal told Cole that Kushner promised bin Zayed he would push the UAE's agenda with Trump if the Emiratis joined the fund. Such slush funds are routine for the Gulf monarchies, the source said: "A billion or two is nothing for them."

Kushner's lawyer denied that he had any knowledge of or connection to the charity, its then-director Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi, or any UAE bank account, and said he complied with all legal requirements in dealing with foreign governments.

By the spring of 2018, Cole writes, bin Zayed had moved roughly another $1 billion to Israel, again via Azerbaijan. A person briefed on the arrangement said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu encouraged Kushner to keep it at Israel's central bank, which handles only government money, where it would look like a government account.

Netanyahu required Kushner to notify him before making any transactions, Cole writes, with messages relayed through then-U.S. Ambassador David Friedman. A person who helped Kushner move money out of Israel told Cole much of it went to accounts in Cyprus.

Friedman denied any knowledge of UAE money for Kushner or passing messages on his behalf. "I know absolutely nothing about any of these allegations," he said, calling the claims about his own role "100% false." Cole acknowledges it is unclear whether the Dutch ever saw this second account.

Cole also describes a third account. As Kushner helped negotiate a secret Israeli commitment to defend the UAE from a major Iranian attack, the Emiratis allegedly sent another transfer to Israel's central bank to cover the cost - a rainy-day defense fund.

As a White House employee with access to classified information, Kushner was required to disclose any account on which he was a signatory or beneficiary. Cole says four senior Trump administration officials - two national security advisers, a White House chief of staff and a CIA director - knew of no presidential authorization for him to access a foreign government's bank account.

A former Mueller prosecutor said that if Kushner promised the royals anything in return - even just a word with his father-in-law - he may have violated federal bribery law and the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Kushner's lawyer said he broke no laws while in the White House, and that every arrangement he made with foreign leaders was agreed to by Trump and in America's interest.

Not the first Gulf windfall

In May 2017, Kushner's sister Nicole Kushner Meyer pitched Chinese investors in Beijing on One Journal Square, a Kushner Companies tower in Jersey City seeking money through the EB-5 program, in which a $500,000 investment buys a path to a green card. She told the room her brother had left the business to join the Trump administration, and the company later apologized.

In February 2018, The Washington Post reported that officials from the UAE, China, Israel and Mexico had privately discussed exploiting Kushner's business dealings and inexperience, with Emirati officials viewing him as particularly manipulable. His security clearance was downgraded around the same time.

Trump ordered chief of staff John Kelly to grant Kushner a top-secret clearance anyway, over the concerns of career intelligence officials and White House counsel Don McGahn, The New York Times reported in 2019 - weeks after Trump told the paper he had not intervened.

In 2017, Kushner Companies reportedly sought a billion-dollar bailout from Qatari officials while Kushner advised Trump to back the Saudi-led blockade of Qatar, according to Senate Finance Democrats. The next year, Brookfield rescued 666 Fifth Avenue with a $1.3 billion, 99-year lease. Qatar's sovereign wealth fund was a major Brookfield backer, though the firm said Qatari representatives had no involvement, and Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Joaquin Castro later probed whether the deal shaped Trump's Qatar policy.

Six months after Kushner left the White House, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund put $2 billion into his new firm, Affinity Partners - overruling its own screening panel, which had flagged the "inexperience" of Kushner's team and called its operations "unsatisfactory in all aspects," The New York Times reported. The fund is run by bin Salman.

By 2024, roughly 99% of Affinity's money came from foreign sources, mainly the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar, according to Wyden, then the Senate Finance chairman, who said those governments were paying Kushner tens of millions of dollars in fees a year. In September 2025, Affinity joined PIF and Silver Lake in a $55 billion deal to take Electronic Arts private.

Kushner is now back inside the administration as Trump's special envoy. In March, Wyden - who had already referred Kushner to the Justice Department over possible foreign-agent violations - and House Oversight's top Democrat, Robert Garcia, demanded answers about Kushner soliciting billions from Gulf sovereign wealth funds while co-leading U.S. Middle East negotiations. Wyden said Kushner is "on the payroll of the Saudi government."
